author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Domestic Violence and Femicide in Afghanistan: Women Are Denied Protection and Justice
content:
Domestic violence has intensified under Taliban rule since August 2021, as the regime has imposed more than 160 edicts and directives restricting the rights and freedoms of women and girls. By barring women from education and employment, severely limiting their freedom of movement, and denying them meaningful access to justice, the Taliban has deepened women’s dependence on their families and left many with fewer ways to escape abuse or seek protection. In this climate of systemic oppression and impunity, domestic violence can go unchallenged, while women and girls face the devastating risk of femicide.

Reports from The Guardian and Zan Times have recorded 231 cases of femicide across just ten provinces -there are 34 provinces – in Afghanistan since 2021. However, it is important to note that these reports emphasized the fact that these cases of femicide do not represent all of the cases in the country since 2021, given the fact that it’s difficult to record these instances of domestic violence after the Taliban has removed avenues to report these crimes.

The Taliban has dismantled the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the prosecutor’s office that handled violence against women, and women’s shelters all together. Additionally, women judges and men judges that were trained on domestic violence issues and supported women, have all been removed. With the Taliban’s return to power, ro

author: Lillian Kollross
title: Texas Mother Sues Anti-Abortion Extremists Under Law Targeting Abortion Pills
content:
Last week, a Texas mother sued Kristan Hawkins, the president and founder of Students for Life of America, an anti-abortion organization, and three other staff members for breaking a law the group helped to establish.

In March 2026, Hawkins posted an Instagram photo with two other staff members in front of the Space Center Houston with the caption: “Guess what we are doing? Ordering abortion pills undercover? Yep. Stay tuned.”

The lawsuit was filed on Oct. 6 by Maria Puerto, who is using a pseudonym to protect her family. Ms. Puerto believes that the group violated House Bill 7, known as the Woman and Child Protection Act, and also mocked those Texans who were deeply affected by the bill.

In December 2025, the Texas legislature passed the Woman and Child Protection Act, which allows almost anyone to sue a person who imports, delivers, or prescribes abortion pills. Plaintiffs can win at least $100,000 per violation.

Despite being on birth control, in 2022, Puerto became pregnant. This unplanned pregnancy came right after Texas banned abortions. With no money or way to travel out of state, along with caring for her disabled mother, Puerto was unable to get an abortion and was forced to carry to term.

author: Sofia Little
title: Election Day is Not the Only Day to Vote
content:
October 24th is Vote Early Day, meant to encourage all eligible United States citizens to vote early and inform voters of their states’ early voting laws.

Early voting offers many voters the convenience and flexibility that match the demands of modern life. It can be especially helpful for people with demanding work schedules, long commutes, caregiving responsibilities or travel plans. For many, the option to vote early can make the difference between casting a ballot and missing the opportunity.

According to the Center for Election and Research (CEIR) nearly 97% of voting-age citizens live in states that offer at least one way to vote before Election Day.

However, access to the ballot remains a concern ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The Trump administration has deployed a wide variety of intensified voter suppression tactics in an attempt to interfere with the 2026 midterm elections. These tactics range from plans to place federal officials at polling stations and an executive order targeting mail voting. Courts have blocked aspects of the administration’s mail voting order from taking effect.

The impact of these voter suppression maneuvers often harm communities of color. Strict voter ID laws and fewer polling locations in certain areas disproportionately affect voters of color, leading to longer wait times on Election Day and discriminatory intimidation tactics at

author: Kiara Green
title: Beyond Indigenous Peoples Day: The Fight to Protect Indigenous Communities
content:
The second Monday in October is federally recognized as Christopher Columbus Day, commemorating the arrival of colonizer Christopher Columbus to the Americas. It’s undeniable that Indigenous communities lived in America long before Columbus docked his ship. Why, then, is he celebrated as the man who “discovered” America?

For years, public debate has challenged this Eurocentric narrative. In response, several states have recognised the second Monday in October as Indigenous Peoples Day. The day celebrates the resilience and the vibrant cultures of Indigenous communities in America.

Despite the lack of federal recognition, Indigenous Peoples Day continues to be celebrated while bringing attention to issues that Indigenous communities face. The day has been used to advocate for the removal of Columbus memorials, the returning of Indigenous lands, and awareness about Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW).

The Trump administration has rejected this broader recognition. In 2025, Trump declared he was “bringing Columbus Day back from the ashes,” reinforcing the federal emphasis on celebrating Columbus rather than recognizing Indigenous peoples.

author: Bianca Blell
title: Women and Girls Severely Affected in Colombia’s 7.4 Earthquake
content:
On August 10th, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicenter near San José del Palmar in the department of Chocó. It was the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in a decade. The disaster damaged homes and essential infrastructure across multiple departments, displacing residents and disrupting access to health care and other critical services.

Chocó, which has a large Afro-Colombian population, was among the hardest-hit areas. During this catastrophic tragedy, where 335 people died, 4,611 people were injured, and which left 111 people missing, it remains the country’s deadliest earthquake since the 1990s.

Though spread out through other nations and departments, most deaths occurred in Valle del Cauca and Risaralda, as the earthquake caused severe humanitarian and protection challenges for vulnerable populations, especially girls and women. More than 31,460 homes were destroyed. 4,996 community centers and 348 health facilities were affected due to conditions from the event. This large scale loss of housing, displacement, and disruption from essential networks have heightened risk of Gender-Based Violence (GBV), especially in rural communities.

author: Halie Moses
title: The Z Factor: Young Voters and the 2026 Midterms
content:
Generation Z voters (aged 18-29) are predicted to make a significant impact on the upcoming 2026 Midterm elections. This has not always been the case, as student and youth voter turnout has historically remained low. Only 47% of Americans aged 18-29 voted in the 2024 election. This year, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote.

In October, a report by UCLA’s William Institute examined the political priorities and voting intentions of Gen Z adults ahead of the 2026 midterms. The study found that nearly 74 percent of respondents said they were likely or certain to vote. These numbers come as no surprise to those who work with students, spend time organizing on college campuses, or identify as Gen Z during the Trump Administration. Rising living costs, ICE raids, attacks on reproductive rights access, sexual assault cases, climate change, and unwanted wars have directly impacted their lives and are driving them to the polls with a passion for change.

Leela Strong, Director of CIRCLE, who works to empower the youth vote, reflected: “Young people are sending us clear signals, not only of dissatisfaction with our politics and deep economic concerns, but also of a strong desire to take action and drive change.” Organizations such as When We All Vote are working to engage young people by connecting their priorities with the issues and candidates on their ballots. author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: California Takes Action to Address Housing Barriers for Survivors
content:
More than one in three women and one in six men in the United States have experienced sexual violence, physical violence and/or stalking by an intimate partner in their lifetime. For survivors trying to leave abusive relationships, finding safe, stable housing can be a major obstacle.

The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), first enacted in 1994, established federal resources to address domestic violence and sexual assault. In the decades since, advocates and policymakers have worked to expand protections and services for survivors. However, access to these resources remains uneven, and recent reductions in federal funding have placed additional pressure on organizations that provide critical support.

From 2020 to 2024, violent crimes involving domestic relationships have increased by 1.9%, disrupting the consecutive decline in violence we saw in previous years. One factor we can attribute this to is the dramatic decline of the federal Victims of Crime Fund. This fund ensures countless crisis centers across the country serve their communities. In its depletion, the numbers speak for themselves.

So what are states doing about it?

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Mail-In Ballots are Safe, For Now
content:
As early voting gets underway in many states, voters can continue to rely on existing mail-in voting procedures for the 2026 midterm elections. On September 14, the US Supreme Court declined to allow the Trump administration to implement new restrictions that would have given the USPS a greater role in determining which voters could receive mail-in ballots. The decision left a lower court order blocking the restrictions in place, allowing states to continue using their existing systems for the November election.

The ruling followed Trump’s Executive Order 14399, issued in March 2026, which took effect in August 2026. The Executive Order required states to adopt a “uniform envelope style” and to submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. It gave the USPS the authority to refuse to deliver ballots to noncompliant states. In its appeal to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued that additional measures like this were needed to preserve election integrity, but that claim was disputed.

Concerns also emerged about whether the new system could function reliably before the midterm elections. A whistleblower report revealed that ballots may never be sent because of systemic and programmatic flaws. author: FMF Staff
title: ICC Arrest Warrants Challenge the Normalization of Taliban Rule and Gender Persecution
content:
On October 5, the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed arrest warrants for four senior Taliban officials. They include Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada, Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Education Minister Habibullah Agha, and Higher Education Minister Neda Mohammad Nadim. The warrants were issued in July 2025 but had remained sealed.

The ICC says there are reasonable grounds to believe the four are criminally responsible for the “crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds against girls, women, and others who do not conform to the Taliban’s policies on gender, gender identity, or expression.” The crimes include conduct involving murder, imprisonment, torture, rape, and enforced disappearance.

The Court also found that Taliban decrees and edicts have severely deprived women and girls of fundamental rights, including education, privacy and family life, as well as freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience, and religion. Importantly, the Court recognized that gender persecution can encompass not only direct acts of violence, but also systemic and institutionalized forms of harm.

author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: Ovarian Cancer Awareness Month Has Ended, ​​But the Need for Research Remains
content:
September marked Ovarian Cancer Awareness Month, but the need for greater research, better treatment, and improved early detection does not end when the month does. Ovarian cancer is expected to cause nearly 14,000 deaths in the US this year. Despite the burden of the disease, detecting ovarian cancer early remains a significant challenge.

Ovarian cancer is actually the deadliest cancer among women and the number one cause of gynecologic cancer deaths. Additionally, only 15% of patients are diagnosed in early stages. Meaning the vast majority of individuals are diagnosed in advanced stages, their survival rate of 30.8%. This tragic reality is largely due to a lack of early detection testing.

Other cancers, such as breast cancer, have preventive measures, such as mammograms routinely recommended; so what’s preventing ovarian cancer from having similar life-saving services?

Breast cancer is the most funded women’s health condition, surpassing ovarian cancer funding levels by billions. Over a span of 25 years, the federal government funded prostate cancer 5.5 times more than ovarian cancer, allocating $276.5 million to the ovarian and $1.53 billion to the prostate.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: New Poll Finds Voters Concerned about Rights and Democracy Ahead of 2026 Midterms
content:
A new national poll from The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights finds that voters are increasingly concerned about threats to their rights, democracy, and the 2026 elections. The 2026 Civil Rights Monitor found that 82% of voters are concerned that rights and freedoms are being taken away or rolled back, the highest level recorded in the five-year history of the poll.

The poll, conducted by Brilliant Corners Research, surveyed 1,000 likely voters by phone between August 23 and September 6. It found that concerns about democracy are also at a series high, with 76% of voters saying they believe democracy is under a major threat. At the same time, voters report high motivation to participate in the upcoming midterm elections, with 84% saying they plan to definitely vote in November.

Protecting the freedom to vote was rated as the top civil rights priority, receiving the highest importance rating among white, Black, Hispanic, and Asian American voters as well as among Democrats and Republicans. Overall, 14% of voters identified voting rights as their top issue, tying it with border security and ranking ahead of abortion rights, which 10% selected.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Addressing the Economic Costs of Sexual Violence: The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act
content:
On September 15, 2026, Rep. Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (NM-03), and Rep. Deborah Ross (NC-02) introduced the Survivors Rights Restitution Act. This legislation would establish a federal restitution program for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government. The bill would include survivors of abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell while addressing the financial burden that can occur from sexual violence.

The bill focuses on the economic consequences that survivors can face long after an assault. The estimated lifetime cost of rape at $122,461 per victim, including the expenses of medical care, loss of income, housing instability and mental health support. These expenses can become an additional burden for survivors as they recover from trauma. The proposed restitution program would provide compensation for certain economic and non-economic harms and losses.

Under the legislation, an independent Office of Special Adjudicators for Survivors Restitution would be established within the US Court of Federal Claims. The office would review petitions from survivors and determine awards through what the bill describes as a streamlined, non-adversarial and trauma-informed process. author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Afghan Women Are Restricted, But They Cannot Be Silenced. They Continue to Be Agents of Change in Afghanistan.
content:
Afghan women have been living under one of the most repressive systems in the world, as the Taliban continue to impose restrictive edicts – over 160 in total to date. These orders restrict their ability to work, attend school, move freely and even leave their homes without a male guardian. Yet despite the barriers the Taliban have imposed, Afghan women continue to be at the forefront of efforts to build peace and stability in Afghanistan.

Peace and security extends beyond just political conversations. They also include the “daily strategies Afghan women employ to defend human rights and generate conditions for peace.” According to a report by the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace, and Security, 81% of Afghan women participate in efforts focused on women’s and girl’s education, 64% in economic empowerment, and another 54% in health & reproductive rights and services. Afghan women are also engaged in health and reproductive rights and services, by roughly 9%, compared to women from other regions of South Asia.

These figures demonstrate the perseverance, leadership, and problem solving of Afghan women. Afghanistan is facing a reproductive health crisis, with maternal mortality rapidly increasing since the Taliban took over in 2021. author: Kiara Green
title: 2026 Midterm Elections: A Guide to Voting and Making an Informed Choice
content:
With Election Day less than 40 days away, voters across the country are preparing to cast ballots in the 2026 midterm elections. On November 3, voters will decide congressional, state, and local races, and ballot measures in states across the country.

With so many races and issues on the same ballot, it is crucial that citizens are making informed decisions when they cast their ballot. Voters may encounter campaign advertisements, social media posts, news coverage, and information from candidates themselves, making it difficult to find a clear overview of where candidates stand on the issues.

One resource that can help is guides.vote, a non-partisan voter guide that provides information about candidates and their stances on a range of issues.

Guides.vote produces nonpartisan voter guides with the help of experienced editors, researchers, and veteran journalists. The guides provide information about candidates’ positions on issues and are designed to help voters compare candidates before casting their ballots.

These guides are available digitally and in print and are offered in both English or Spanish. Guides.vote currently includes 2026 election information for races in states across the country.

author: Sofia Little
title: Get the Flock Out
content:
On September 23rd, the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held a hearing titled “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” examining the privacy risks, data sharing, and misuse of private automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks.

The hearing was chaired by Sen. Hawley (R-MO) and featured five witnesses, including Lindsey Isaacs, a wrongfully accused driver, Alasdair Whitney from Legislative Counsel Institute for Justice, Sheriff Ross Teeple, Benn Jordan, a self-proclaimed “hacker”, and policy counsel analyst Chad Marlow from the ACLU, where they have coined a campaign called “Get the Flock Out.”

The hearing highlighted pertinent concerns about how ALPR technology can be used and shared. Public concern about Flock cameras has also grown in recent months. A September 2026 Navigator Research survey found that 62% of registered voters were concerned about Flock camera use, including 66% of Democrats, 55% of Republicans, and 70% of Independents.

Flock Safety was founded in 2017 by CEO Garrett Langley, operating as a small startup meant to provide ALPR cameras to homeowners associations and neighborhoods looking to reduce petty theft and local property crimes. author: Bianca Blell
title: Virginia Voters Will Decide the Future of Reproductive Freedom, Marriage Equality, and Voting Rights This November
content:
On November 3rd, Virginia voters will decide on three proposed amendments to the state constitution concerning reproductive freedom, marriage, and voting rights. The amendments would add a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, remove Virginia’s constitutional prohibition on same-sex marriage and require equal treatment of marriages, and automatically restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon release of incarceration.

Together, the measures represent one of the most consequential ballot slates for civil rights in the state’s recent history, including a rare opportunity for voters to enshrine protections directly into the state constitution, beyond the reach of a hostile legislature or a change in administration. All three amendments were approved by the General Assembly through Virginia’s constitutional amendment process and will appear on the November 2026 ballot.

The first amendment establishes a constitutional right to reproductive freedom and access. The amendment defines the right as including decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management, and fertility care. It would also prohibit the Commonwealth from penalizing or prosecuting individuals for exercising those rights, as well as doctors, nurses, and others who assist patients with their voluntary consent.

author: FMF Staff
title: Five Years Later, Girls in Afghanistan Are Still Waiting For School Doors To Open
content:
For five years, girls above sixth grade have been barred from classrooms, making Afghanistan the only country in the world where girls are banned from secondary and higher education.

The ban was initially said to be a temporary measure but has now defined half a decade of life for millions of Afghan girls. For them, these years were supposed to be spent in classrooms, preparing for university, building careers, and planning their futures. Instead, they have been spending time waiting.

According to United Nations data, 2.6 million girls have been denied their right to education since the ban began, a policy that experts warn will have long-term consequences not only for girls, but for Afghanistan’s economy, health system, and future development. UNICEF has warned that if the ban continues, millions more girls will be deprived of education by the end of the decade. The ban has already dismantled the pipeline for female doctors and midwives. The maternal and infant mortality rate has already gone up and is only expected to go higher.

When looking beyond the statistics, we see the actual lives that have been put on pause for 5 years.
